sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 490 BCE an Achaemenid expedition under Datis and Artaphernes crossed the Aegean and reached Attica.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The expedition sought to subdue Athens and Eretria. These were imperial objectives, wider than a single battlefield.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Athens needed to preserve its independence; the expedition needed political submission as well as military success.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Marathon was a coastal plain in northeastern Attica. Herodotus describes it as suitable for cavalry.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Athenian and Plataean infantry opposed the Persian expedition. Athenian command included Miltiades and the polemarch Callimachus.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Herodotus describes stronger Greek wings and a shallower center. This is a literary account, not a surveyed deployment.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The narrative moves from an advance to fighting in the center, success on the wings, and a struggle near the ships.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Committing to battle involved accepting risk without certainty about Persian intentions. The surviving narrative cannot recover a commander's private reasoning.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Greek wings prevailed while their center gave ground; the wings then converged against the remaining Persian troops.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Persian force withdrew by sea. The Athenians returned to protect Athens.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle became a durable civic memory: the Marathon museum preserves finds associated with the Athenian and Plataean burial mounds.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Compare battlefield success with the continuing task of defending the city. A successful engagement does not remove every operational threat.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Persian cavalry activity and exact troop positions are unresolved here. Accounts of Datis's fate conflict; a schematic must not imply certainty.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Read Herodotus as a later Greek narrative, Iranica for Datis and source criticism, and the archaeological museum for material context.

phases.title: Opposing armies
phases.description: The expedition and Greek defenders face one another on the Marathon plain.

phases.title: Center under pressure
phases.description: In Herodotus's account, the Persian center advances against the thinner Greek center.

phases.title: Wings converge
phases.description: The successful Greek wings turn toward the remaining enemy.

phases.title: Return to Athens
phases.description: The defenders return while the Persian fleet sails around the coast.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Edward the Confessor's death opened a disputed succession. Harold became king; William of Normandy claimed the crown.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Harold defeated the Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge before returning south to face William's landing in Sussex.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: William needed to defeat the reigning king to advance his claim. Harold needed to contain an invader while preserving royal authority.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The English held a ridge near the modern town of Battle. The battlefield's exact extent remains uncertain.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Harold's army fought on foot, including household warriors. William's army used infantry, archers and mounted troops.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The English occupied the ridge in a defensive formation; William's forces approached from rising ground to the south.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Repeated assaults lasted throughout 14 October 1066. A Norman retreat and rally preceded renewed attacks.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: William rallied his troops after a report that he had died. English pursuit during retreats exposed parts of their formation.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The interaction of lost cohesion and repeated pressure matters more than explaining the result through a single weapon.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Harold was killed and his army broken. William was crowned on Christmas Day.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory opened the Norman conquest and transformed England's political relationship with continental Europe.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Distinguish an army's tactical position from the wider demands of defending a kingdom against successive invasions.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Bayeux Tapestry and written narratives leave details unresolved. This account does not specify Harold's exact fatal wound or precise unit positions.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: English Heritage summarizes the narrative and material setting. Historic England documents the registered battlefield and surviving source problems.

phases.title: The ridge
phases.description: Harold's infantry holds the higher ground.

phases.title: Assault and rally
phases.description: William's forces attack; the duke restores confidence during a retreat.

phases.title: Repeated pressure
phases.description: Further attacks and pursuits disrupt sections of the English formation.

phases.title: Collapse
phases.description: Harold's death accompanies the defeat of his army.

perspectives.name: William, Duke of Normandy
perspectives.objective: Defeat Harold in battle to make good his claim to the English crown.
perspectives.known: Harold had come south after Stamford Bridge, and the English held a strong position on a ridge.
perspectives.uncertainty: How long the English shield wall could hold, and whether his own army would stay together under repeated repulses.
perspectives.constraints: An invading army in hostile country, dependent on its ships and on foraging.
perspectives.forces: Norman, Breton and other French troops, combining infantry, archers and mounted warriors.
perspectives.terrain: His army attacked uphill from rising ground to the south of the English position.
perspectives.logistics: The army was sustained from its base near Hastings and by foraging in Sussex.
perspectives.decision: He launched repeated assaults and, in the narratives, rallied his troops after a rumor of his death. Whether later Norman retreats were deliberate feints is debated.
perspectives.outcome: Harold was killed and his army broken. William was crowned on Christmas Day 1066.

perspectives.name: Harold II of England
perspectives.objective: Defeat or contain the invasion and preserve his kingship.
perspectives.known: William had landed at Pevensey. Harold's own army had just fought at Stamford Bridge in Yorkshire.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether more troops would join him if he waited, and what William would do in the meantime.
perspectives.constraints: Losses and fatigue after Stamford Bridge and a hurried march south.
perspectives.forces: Household warriors and other troops fighting on foot in a shield wall.
perspectives.terrain: The ridge gave a strong defensive position but little room to maneuver.
perspectives.logistics: The rapid march from Yorkshire left little time to gather fresh forces.
perspectives.decision: He gave battle quickly near Hastings instead of waiting for a larger army. Historians debate whether he meant to fight at once or to pin William near the coast.
perspectives.outcome: His death and the collapse of his army opened the way to the Norman conquest.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 1415 Henry V of England invaded Normandy and besieged and took Harfleur. He then resolved to march through northern France to English-held Calais.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Henry pressed a claim to the French throne, which the victory later strengthened. The French king summoned men-at-arms from across the kingdom, and a royal council resolved to give battle, while France's princes remained divided by their own conflicts.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Henry needed to bring his army safely to Calais. The French aimed to intercept and destroy it before it got there.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Barred from the Somme ford at Blanchetaque, the English crossed further upstream and were met near Azincourt. They advanced from Maisoncelles over fields recently sown with corn, with Tramecourt to one side. Record-based research argues the ground could not have held the very large French army of popular accounts.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Anne Curry's study of English and French financial records suggests roughly 8,500–9,000 English and about 12,000 French, a much smaller gap than the chronicles imply. Most of Henry's army were archers, and Welsh soldiers were a small share. The French command was shared among the constable, the marshal and several great princes.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Monstrelet describes the French in a vanguard, main body and rearguard, with mounted wings to strike the English flanks. The vanguard was led by the constable with the dukes of Orléans and Bourbon and Marshal Boucicaut. The English placed archers in front, each with a sharpened stake, men-at-arms behind and horses and baggage to the rear.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On Friday 25 October the French waited by their banners. The English advanced and opened with heavy archery. A French mounted attack on the flanks failed, and wounded horses recoiled into the vanguard. Close fighting followed, then a raid on the English baggage, the killing of prisoners and the withdrawal of the French rear.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The French chose to wait for an attack, confident in their numbers, although Monstrelet says some leaders privately feared an open battle. Henry advanced to bring on the fight. When the baggage was attacked and a renewed assault seemed possible, he ordered the prisoners killed.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The failed mounted attack disordered the French vanguard. Pressed together, it could fight only with its front rank, while English archers and men-at-arms struck it.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The English won. Monstrelet lists many French princes and lords among the dead and captured. Henry withdrew to Maisoncelles, then marched to Calais and embarked for England.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory supported Henry's claim to the French throne. The battle later became central to English and British national memory, shaped above all by Shakespeare's Henry V.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Archery from a protected position mattered most against an enemy that was crowded and disordered. The size of an army counted for less than whether it could use its numbers.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Army sizes remain debated: chronicles give far larger French totals than the administrative records. Ransom contracts suggest the killing of prisoners did not spare men by rank. The archers' V sign has no contemporary record, and the Welsh did not form most of the army.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Monstrelet gives a detailed French narrative, but figures such as his 13,000 English archers conflict with record evidence. University of Southampton research uses muster rolls, pay records and ransom contracts to test the chronicles.

phases.title: The armies draw up
phases.description: The French form three divisions and wait; English archers plant stakes in front of the line.

phases.title: English advance
phases.description: The English move forward and open heavy archery; the French mounted flank attack fails.

phases.title: Close combat
phases.description: Recoiling horses disorder the crowded French vanguard, which is defeated hand to hand.

phases.title: Alarm and killing of prisoners
phases.description: A raid on the baggage leads Henry to order prisoners killed; the French rear withdraws.

perspectives.name: Henry V of England
perspectives.objective: Bring his army from Harfleur to Calais and uphold his claim in France.
perspectives.known: A French army had gathered across his route after he was forced away from the Somme ford at Blanchetaque.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the French would attack or simply block his road, and whether his outnumbered army could survive a battle.
perspectives.constraints: An army that had besieged Harfleur and then detoured upstream to cross the Somme, far from its base.
perspectives.forces: Mainly archers with a smaller body of men-at-arms; record evidence suggests about 8,500–9,000 men.
perspectives.terrain: Open fields recently sown with corn between Maisoncelles, Azincourt and Tramecourt.
perspectives.logistics: Horses and baggage were kept to the rear, where a French raid struck them.
perspectives.decision: He advanced to provoke an attack, with archers protected by stakes, and later ordered the prisoners killed when a renewed attack seemed possible.
perspectives.outcome: A decisive victory, after which he continued to Calais and returned to England.

perspectives.name: Charles d'Albret, constable of France
perspectives.objective: Stop the English army before it reached Calais, as the royal council had resolved.
perspectives.known: The English army was smaller and had been marching through hostile country.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether waiting or attacking would serve better; Monstrelet says some leaders privately feared an open battle.
perspectives.constraints: Command of the vanguard was shared with royal dukes and other great lords. This analysis infers rather than documents how far that limited his authority.
perspectives.forces: Men-at-arms, archers and crossbowmen in three divisions with mounted wings; record evidence suggests about 12,000 men.
perspectives.terrain: Recently sown fields where the vanguard became crowded once the fighting began.
perspectives.logistics: Men-at-arms summoned from across the kingdom to intercept the English march.
perspectives.decision: The French waited in position, then sent mounted wings against the English flanks before the vanguard closed.
perspectives.outcome: The vanguard was defeated; Monstrelet lists many French princes and lords killed or captured.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By 1863 the Union had gained ground on most fronts: Grant was besieging Vicksburg and the navy was blockading Southern ports. The Eastern Theater remained the Confederacy's main success, and after victory at Chancellorsville in May Lee decided to invade the North.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The National Park Service describes Lee's aims as raising Confederate morale, easing pressure on Vicksburg, drawing the Union army onto better ground, gathering supplies from Pennsylvania farms and winning victories that might push the Union toward peace.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Lee's plan included destroying the Susquehanna bridge at Harrisburg and disabling the Pennsylvania Railroad. Lincoln and Halleck ordered the Army of the Potomac to stay between Lee and Washington; on 28 June George Meade replaced Joseph Hooker in command.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: After 1 July the Union held high ground south of the town in a fishhook-shaped line from Culp's Hill through Cemetery Hill and Cemetery Ridge to Little Round Top. The Confederates formed a longer, outer arc along Seminary Ridge about a mile away, with open fields between.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Lee commanded the Army of Northern Virginia, with corps under Longstreet, Ewell and Hill. Meade commanded the Army of the Potomac, which he had led for only a few days. Stuart's cavalry was out of contact with Lee as the armies converged.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Learning that Union forces had crossed the Potomac, Lee concentrated near Cashtown, west of Gettysburg. Heth's division approached along the Chambersburg Pike while Buford's Union cavalry approached from the south. Neither commander expected to fight at Gettysburg.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 1 July Confederates attacked on McPherson Ridge and drove Union troops through the town to Cemetery Hill. On 2 July Lee attacked both Union flanks. On 3 July Union troops retook works on Culp's Hill, a two-hour bombardment preceded an assault on the Union centre, and that assault failed. Lee withdrew from 4 July.

refs.locator: The Third Day; End of Invasion

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: At midnight on 2 July Meade's corps commanders advised holding their positions, and he did. Having found the Union flanks strong, Lee attacked the centre on 3 July with about 12,000 men in what became known as Pickett's Charge.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: On the high ground, the Union's shorter interior line let Meade shift troops to threatened points, while Confederate attacks from the outer arc were harder to coordinate. The failure of the 3 July assault ended Lee's hope of victory on this field.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Lee began an orderly retreat late on 4 July, with a long train of wounded. Heavy rain slowed both armies, and the swollen Potomac trapped Lee until the river fell and he crossed into Virginia. Critics charged that Meade had let the Confederate army slip away.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Gettysburg's churches, public buildings and homes became hospitals. A Soldiers' National Cemetery was established, and Lincoln spoke at its dedication on 19 November 1863. The war continued until Lee surrendered at Appomattox in April 1865.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An unplanned meeting engagement can commit whole armies to ground neither commander chose. Lee's loss of cavalry reconnaissance shows how gaps in information shape decisions before the fighting starts.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Park Service pages describe Lee's aims with different emphases, and their figures are approximations. Meade's pursuit remains debated. This study does not adopt labels such as "high-water mark" or repeat casualty totals.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Park Service overview and teaching background give the campaign and the three days. The park's historical handbook adds the plan of campaign, Meade's council of war and the retreat.

phases.title: Meeting engagement
phases.description: Confederates attack west of town and drive Union troops back to Cemetery Hill.

phases.title: Attacks on both flanks
phases.description: Longstreet strikes the Union left and Ewell the right; the Union line holds.

phases.title: Assault on the centre
phases.description: After a bombardment, about 12,000 Confederates advance on Cemetery Ridge and are repulsed.

phases.title: Retreat
phases.description: Lee withdraws toward Virginia; Meade pursues but Lee crosses the Potomac when the river falls.

perspectives.name: Robert E. Lee
perspectives.objective: Win a decisive victory on Northern soil that would raise Confederate morale and press the Union toward peace.
perspectives.known: On the night of 28 June an agent reported that the Union army had crossed the Potomac and was close.
perspectives.uncertainty: With Stuart's cavalry out of contact, he had little reconnaissance of Union strength and positions.
perspectives.constraints: A supply line stretched far from Virginia, and corps that had to concentrate quickly from scattered positions.
perspectives.forces: The Army of Northern Virginia, with corps under Longstreet, Ewell and Hill.
perspectives.terrain: Seminary Ridge, an exterior line facing open fields toward the Union centre.
perspectives.logistics: The army foraged in Pennsylvania farmland; its retreat began with a wagon train of wounded many miles long.
perspectives.decision: He attacked both Union flanks on 2 July and, finding them strong, attacked the centre on 3 July.
perspectives.outcome: The assault failed, and he retreated to Virginia.

perspectives.name: George G. Meade
perspectives.objective: Keep the Army of the Potomac between Lee and Washington and defeat the invasion.
perspectives.known: He took command on 28 June at Frederick, Maryland, only days before the battle.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where Lee would strike next; before 3 July he expected the main attack on his left.
perspectives.constraints: New to army command, with corps arriving at Gettysburg piecemeal after the first day.
perspectives.forces: The Army of the Potomac, whose corps commanders he consulted in a midnight council of war.
perspectives.terrain: High ground in a fishhook-shaped interior line from Culp's Hill to Little Round Top.
perspectives.logistics: Reserve batteries were brought up behind the centre, and the Baltimore Pike ran behind the Union right.
perspectives.decision: He held his positions and kept three corps on his left, while Hancock strengthened the stone wall at the centre; after the battle he pursued Lee.
perspectives.outcome: A defensive victory, followed by criticism that Lee had been allowed to escape.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Viet Minh had fought French forces in northern Vietnam since 1946. The United States, alarmed by communist movements in Asia after 1949, funded the French war. In May 1953 General Henri Navarre took command in Indochina, charged with finding an honourable way out.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Navarre's two-year plan was discussed in Paris but never formally approved, and he received no clear answer on what to do if Laos were threatened. The announcement in February 1954 of a Geneva conference raised the stakes, and Chinese aid to the Viet Minh increased sharply.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Navarre meant the base to protect Laos, draw Viet Minh forces away from the Tonkin delta and support operations. The Viet Minh concentrated to destroy the garrison.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The base lay in a valley near the Laotian border. Its key element was the airfield, surrounded by strongpoints with women's names such as Béatrice, Gabrielle, Anne-Marie and Huguette.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Colonel de Castries commanded a garrison of twelve battalions, whose artillery was commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Piroth. General Giap concentrated several Viet Minh divisions, with artillery and anti-aircraft regiments, around the valley; Nguyễn Trọng Minh notes that the 105 mm howitzer regiment had been equipped and trained in China.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: French and Vietnamese paratroopers dropped into the valley on 20–22 November 1953 in Operation Castor and built an air-ground base. By the end of December the garrison was encircled, while Viet Minh troops dug trenches and tunnels toward its positions. They also dug their guns into the slopes facing the valley, under thick cover and camouflage, while the French guns stood in open emplacements.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Viet Minh artillery opened fire on 13 March 1954. Béatrice and Gabrielle fell within two days, and the airstrip could not be used after 26 March. Fighting for the eastern hills lasted from 30 March to 10 April. The final offensive began on 1 May, and resistance ended on 7 May.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: At a meeting on 26 January 1954, about ten hours before an attack already put back from 20 January was due to open, Giap postponed it, withdrew the guns and changed the plan from “fast attack, fast victory” to “steady attack, steady advance”; Nguyễn Trọng Minh attributes the first plan to the Chinese advisers, and Giap called the change the hardest decision of his career. France reinforced the shrinking garrison by parachuting in volunteers, many of them not trained parachutists. Washington would intervene only as part of a coalition, and Britain and other NATO members declined to join.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of the airfield left a garrison designed around air supply dependent on parachute drops, while the Viet Minh tightened the ring. In the Vietnamese study, French artillery observers and reconnaissance aircraft were lost within the first two days, and anti-aircraft fire forced supply aircraft to drop from high altitude, so that much of the supply fell to the besiegers.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Late on 7 May, de Castries ordered the fighting to stop. About 10,000 men were taken prisoner; the French ministry states that around 60 per cent of them died in Viet Minh camps.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Geneva agreements of July 1954 brought a ceasefire and a temporary division of Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with elections planned for 1956. The United States did not sign the second agreement and backed Ngo Dinh Diem in the South. French rule in Indochina ended.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A base that depends on a single airfield is only as secure as that airfield. An opponent who can bring supplies to a remote place should not be underestimated, and a commander who sees that his plan is not ready may do better to call off the attack than to keep to the timetable.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The U.S. Office of the Historian counts a four-month siege, from the encirclement; the French ministry dates the battle from the 13 March attack. Navarre's unapproved plan leaves responsibility for the decision open, and Viet Minh losses are historians' estimates. Vietnamese scholarship, represented here by Nguyễn Trọng Minh, explains the defeat through French overconfidence, above all Piroth's belief that Viet Minh guns could not be brought to the valley or survive his counter-battery fire, and credits the Vietnamese artillery; the role of the Chinese advisers in the first plan remains a point of interpretation.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The French Ministry of the Armed Forces gives the plan, the course of the siege and its human cost. The U.S. Office of the Historian gives American deliberations and the Geneva settlement. Nguyễn Trọng Minh's article, in Vietnamese, gives the Vietnamese view of the artillery battle, drawing on Giap's memoirs and on French memoirs and histories; its equipment figures are not used.

perspectives.objective: Weaken the Viet Minh enough to allow France an honourable exit from the war.
perspectives.known: His plan had been discussed in Paris, but he had no clear instructions if Laos were threatened.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Viet Minh could concentrate and supply large forces around a remote valley.

perspectives.objective: Destroy the French garrison in the valley.
perspectives.known: The garrison depended on its airfield and was encircled by late December 1953.
perspectives.uncertainty: How long the garrison could be supplied and reinforced by air.
perspectives.constraints: A remote battlefield where heavy weapons, ammunition and fuel had to be brought in overland.
perspectives.forces: Several divisions with artillery and anti-aircraft regiments.
perspectives.terrain: Ground around the valley where trenches and tunnels could be dug toward the French positions.
perspectives.logistics: Chinese aid in weapons, ammunition, trucks and fuel grew sharply from February 1954.
perspectives.decision: He called off the attack planned for late January and withdrew his guns, then opened with artillery on 13 March, took the strongpoints in stages and launched a final offensive on 1 May.
perspectives.outcome: The garrison surrendered on 7 May, and France left Indochina after the Geneva agreements.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: As Han authority collapsed, regional warlords fought for control. By 208 Cao Cao held the North China plain and turned south against Liu Biao, Governor of Jing province, and Sun Quan, who controlled the lower Yangzi.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: De Crespigny notes that when the Later Han was founded, control of the North China plain had decided the civil war, and in 208 most people, including Cao Cao's opponents, expected the pattern to repeat. When Liu Biao died that autumn, his successor Liu Zong surrendered Jing province.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Cao Cao occupied the naval base at Jiangling and called on Sun Quan to surrender. De Crespigny suggests he probably saw the advance as an armed reconnaissance that he could abandon if it failed. Sun Quan sent troops forward to test Cao Cao's strength while keeping a reserve with which to negotiate.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies met at the Red Cliffs on the Yangzi, between present-day Wuhan and Yueyang. The northern troops were unused to southern waterways and marshland. The precise site remains debated; the cliff where Su Shi's boat party of 1082 took place was only traditionally identified with the battle.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Sun Quan's power was a fraction of what Cao Cao could mobilize, but his Yangzi navy was experienced and locally superior. Zhou Yu commanded Sun Quan's forces alongside Liu Bei. Much of Cao Cao's fleet had served Liu Biao, and its loyalty was uncertain. Cao Cao's claim of about 800,000 men is not credible.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Liu Bei tried to hold a line on the Yangzi but was caught and heavily defeated, and turned to Sun Quan. His lieutenant Guan Yu had saved much of the Jing fleet. The allies and Cao Cao's forces then faced each other across the river for several days.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Cao Cao took over Jing province in autumn 208 and pursued Liu Bei eastward with his army and new fleet. At the Red Cliffs his first attack was driven back. When the wind changed, Zhou Yu sent in fireships, and Cao Cao abandoned his position and retreated, leaving garrisons. The following year Zhou Yu captured Jiangling.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: After debate at his headquarters, Sun Quan chose to fight rather than surrender. Zhou Yu used the change of wind for a fire attack, a common weapon of the time, and Cao Cao chose to withdraw rather than fight on.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The fire attack struck an army already worn by forced marches, sickness and uncertain loyalties. A setback became a retreat because Cao Cao's force was not fit for a prolonged river campaign.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Cao Cao retreated north. The allies, in de Crespigny's words, enhanced their victory with tales of slaughter, and Zhou Yu took Jiangling the next year.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The south kept naval control of the middle Yangzi, and later northern attempts to break the river defences failed. De Crespigny judges that the campaign proved to be the last chance for many years to reunite the empire, opening the way to the Three Kingdoms.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Control of a great river and skill on it could offset a large difference in overall strength. An advance meant as a probe can still decide a war if it fails.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: De Crespigny considers Cao Cao's defeat probably exaggerated and the story embellished by later literature, above all the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (chapters 43–50). Popular retellings add episodes such as a chained fleet and Huang Gai's feigned defection, which this study does not treat as established.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The main historical account is the biography of Zhou Yu in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), with Pei Songzhi's commentary. De Crespigny's history is the principal source here; World History Encyclopedia reflects the popular tradition, and Su Shi's essay shows how the battle was remembered.

phases.title: Southern campaign
phases.description: Liu Biao dies, Jing province surrenders and Cao Cao defeats Liu Bei.

phases.title: Alliance on the river
phases.description: Sun Quan sends Zhou Yu to join Liu Bei; the armies face each other across the Yangzi.

phases.title: Fire attack
phases.description: Cao Cao's first attack fails; with a change of wind, fireships drive him from his position.

phases.title: Retreat and Jiangling
phases.description: Cao Cao withdraws north, leaving garrisons; Zhou Yu captures Jiangling the following year.

perspectives.name: Cao Cao
perspectives.objective: Complete the reunification of the empire by subduing Jing province and Sun Quan.
perspectives.known: Jing province had surrendered with its fleet, and Liu Bei had been heavily defeated.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether Sun Quan would surrender, and whether the former Jing troops and sailors would stay loyal.
perspectives.constraints: Troops tired by a long campaign and forced marches, unused to southern waterways and suffering from sickness.
perspectives.forces: His northern army and the fleet taken over from Liu Biao; his claim of about 800,000 men is not credible.
perspectives.terrain: The middle Yangzi and its marshlands.
perspectives.logistics: The captured naval base at Jiangling.
perspectives.decision: He pursued eastward with army and fleet and demanded Sun Quan's surrender, probably treating the advance as an armed reconnaissance.
perspectives.outcome: Driven from his position by a fire attack, he retreated and lost Jiangling the following year.

perspectives.name: Sun Quan
perspectives.objective: Preserve his independent state on the lower Yangzi.
perspectives.known: Cao Cao had taken Jing province and its naval base and was advancing downriver.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether to fight or submit; his headquarters debated the choice at length.
perspectives.constraints: A power only a fraction of Cao Cao's, with an exposed northern flank and inaccessible hill country in the south.
perspectives.forces: An experienced Yangzi navy commanded by Zhou Yu.
perspectives.terrain: The river itself, where his fleet held local superiority.
perspectives.logistics: Control of the Yangzi below Wuhan, the Poyang region and Hangzhou Bay.
perspectives.decision: He sent Zhou Yu forward to join Liu Bei and test Cao Cao's strength, keeping a reserve with which to negotiate if necessary.
perspectives.outcome: Victory secured southern control of the middle Yangzi for many years.

sources.title: Al-Baladhuri: The Battle of the Yarmuk (636) and After
Battle of Yarmūk
sources.publisher: EBSCO Research Starters (Bart L. R. Talbert, 2022)

sources.title: Yarmuk (Encyclopaedia Judaica, 2nd ed.)
sources.publisher: Encyclopedia.com (Michael Avi-Yonah, Abraham J. Brawer and Shaked Gilboa)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Ridda Wars reasserted the caliphate's control of Arabia, Muslim armies advanced into Iraq and Syria; Talbert dates the first raids into Byzantine territory to 629 and Abu Bakr's dispatch of four armies to 633. They defeated a Byzantine army at Ajnadayn in July 634, won at Pella early in 635 and took Damascus and Emesa (Homs) later that year. Both the Byzantine and Sasanian empires were exhausted by their long war with each other.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Emperor Heraclius gathered a large army at Antioch to recover Syria, drawn from Greeks, Syrians, Mesopotamians and Armenians, with Arab tribal contingents under the Ghassanid Jabalah ibn al-Aiham. Britannica's summary says he allied with the Sasanians and played for time while he waited for their forces; Talbert describes him as ill. Al-Baladhuri portrays many Syrians as hostile to Byzantine rule.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Heraclius aimed to drive the Muslim armies out of Syria. The Muslim commanders gave up Emesa, Damascus and their other dispersed positions and concentrated their forces to meet his army in one place; Britannica's summary credits Khalid with arguing for this at a council of war.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought near the Yarmuk River (the ancient Hieromax), on a plateau suited to light cavalry and cut by deep wadis. Behind the Byzantine position, the gorge of the Wadi Ruqqad could be crossed by a single bridge; Talbert has the Byzantines cross by this old Roman bridge to deploy.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Vahan, an Armenian general, commanded the Byzantine field army. Abu Ubaidah held the Muslim command in Syria; World History Encyclopedia and Talbert say he left battlefield direction to Khalid ibn al-Walid. Al-Baladhuri claims about 200,000 Byzantine troops against 24,000 Muslims; modern estimates are far lower, Talbert judges that the armies were probably close to equal by the time they met, and no reliable count survives.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Muslim forces withdrew from Palestine, Jordan and Emesa to the Yarmuk plateau and were reinforced from Medina. The armies then faced each other for months of negotiation and build-up before fighting began. Talbert describes the Byzantines in four divisions and Khalid's army in four infantry and four cavalry divisions, with a larger cavalry reserve behind them.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: World History Encyclopedia dates the battle to six days, 15–20 August 636, and Talbert also opens it on 15 August; Britannica's summary instead begins it on 20 August, the date the Encyclopaedia Judaica gives for the battle, and al-Baladhuri dates it to Rajab of the year 15 AH. After opening duels, Byzantine attacks pushed the Muslim flanks back to their camps, where, in Muslim tradition, the women rallied the men. A cavalry reserve restored the line, and on the last day a Muslim envelopment broke the Byzantine army.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: According to World History Encyclopedia, Khalid refused a truce Vahan requested on the fifth day, sent cavalry at night to seize the bridge over the Wadi Ruqqad and then led massed cavalry around the Byzantine left. Talbert has the mounted reserve strike the Byzantine flanks and cut their infantry off from their cavalry, and names its commander, Zarrar, as the man who took the bridge.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Holding the only bridge in the Byzantine rear turned a defeat into the destruction of the army, since the flank attack drove it toward ground with no escape. Britannica's summary and the Encyclopaedia Judaica add that a wind carrying sand from the desert blew at the Muslims' backs.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Byzantine army was destroyed; many were driven into the gorges of the Yarmuk and the Ruqqad, and survivors fled toward Palestine, Antioch, Aleppo, Mesopotamia and Armenia. Al-Baladhuri reports that Heraclius left Antioch for Constantinople and bade farewell to Syria.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Syria passed permanently to the caliphate, and Jerusalem surrendered in 637; by 645, Talbert notes, Syria, Palestine and Egypt were under Muslim rule, with Christians and Jews tolerated. Al-Baladhuri describes the people of Hims opening their gates and paying tribute. Heraclius turned to the defence of Anatolia and Egypt, and Khalid was removed from command soon after his victory.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A mobile reserve and control of the enemy's line of retreat can matter more than numbers. Talbert's judgement is that the Byzantines gambled everything on one decisive battle instead of their usual caution. Local attitudes to imperial rule shaped what followed the battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Al-Baladhuri died around 892, so the detailed narratives come from two centuries after the battle, and Arab chroniclers tended to inflate enemy numbers. Modern accounts disagree even on the dates and on how many days were spent fighting. The sources differ on Jabalah: al-Baladhuri places him with the Byzantines and has him convert only later, while some accounts report a defection during the battle, and Talbert speaks of desertions and infighting among the Byzantine contingents. Talbert treats the rally by the women as a Muslim tradition. Vahan's fate is uncertain.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan gives an early Islamic account built from episodes and anecdotes. World History Encyclopedia gives a modern reconstruction drawing on works such as David Nicolle's study of the battle. Talbert's research starter follows the standard modern studies, including Donner, Kaegi and Jandora's reconstruction, but is not free of inconsistencies; the Encyclopaedia Judaica entry and Britannica's summary are short.

phases.title: Armies gather
phases.description: Muslim forces concentrate on the Yarmuk plateau; Heraclius's army arrives and negotiations begin.

phases.title: Byzantine assaults
phases.description: Byzantine attacks drive the Muslim flanks back to their camps; a cavalry reserve restores the line.

phases.title: Closing the bridge
phases.description: Muslim cavalry seizes the bridge over the Wadi Ruqqad behind the Byzantine army.

phases.title: Envelopment and rout
phases.description: A massed cavalry attack turns the Byzantine left; the army breaks with no line of escape.

perspectives.name: Vahan
perspectives.objective: Destroy the Muslim army and restore Byzantine rule in Syria.
perspectives.known: The Muslim forces had given up their scattered positions and concentrated on the Yarmuk plateau.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether a large army of many peoples and allied contingents would hold together in a long battle.
perspectives.constraints: World History Encyclopedia and Britannica's summary say the Byzantines delayed to coordinate with the Sasanians, giving their opponents time to concentrate and reinforce.
perspectives.forces: Troops from across the empire and its allies, including Armenians and Ghassanid Arabs.
perspectives.terrain: A line anchored on a gorge and hills, with the Wadi Ruqqad and a single bridge behind it.
perspectives.logistics: The army had been gathered at Antioch, far to the north.
perspectives.decision: He made repeated attacks over several days, then asked for a truce on the fifth day.
perspectives.outcome: His army was destroyed; whether he died in the battle is uncertain.

perspectives.name: Khalid ibn al-Walid
perspectives.objective: Defeat the Byzantine field army and secure Syria.
perspectives.known: According to World History Encyclopedia, his scouts warned of a Byzantine dawn attack.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether an outnumbered army could hold its line against repeated assaults.
perspectives.constraints: He was not the formal commander; Abu Ubaidah was ready to accept the Byzantine truce.
perspectives.forces: An army in which light cavalry formed a mobile reserve, reinforced from Medina.
perspectives.terrain: A flat plateau suited to cavalry, and a gorge behind the enemy with only one crossing.
perspectives.logistics: Reinforcements reached the army from Medina before the battle.
perspectives.decision: He refused the truce, seized the bridge by night and led the cavalry around the Byzantine left.
perspectives.outcome: A decisive victory, after which he was nevertheless removed from command.

sources.title: De Expugnatione Terrae Sanctae per Saladinum: The Battle of Hattin, 1187 (trans. James Brundage)
The Battle of Hattin (1187): three accounts (trans. Peter W. Edbury)
Some Medieval Accounts of Salah al-Din's Recovery of Jerusalem (Al-Quds)
sources.publisher: Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University (Hadia Dajani-Shakeel)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By 1187 Saladin had made the recovery of Jerusalem a central aim. The Latin kingdom of Jerusalem under King Guy of Lusignan was divided by rivalries among its nobles.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Saladin gathered a large army east of the Jordan. Guy, now reconciled with Count Raymond III of Tripoli, assembled the kingdom's forces at the springs of Saffuriya with the Templars, Hospitallers and leading barons, using money from Henry II of England to hire mercenaries.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Saladin besieged Tiberias on 2 July, while the Countess Eschiva held out in the citadel and appealed for help. Guy's council resolved to march to relieve the town. Saladin's aim of drawing the army away from water is an interpretation of his actions, not a documented intention.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Between Saffuriya and the lake of Tiberias lay dry ground in high summer. The army was eventually forced onto the Horns of Hattin, near a village whose water it never reached.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Frankish army combined the royal host, the military orders and hired troops; De Expugnatione claims 1,200 knights and 18,000 or more infantry. Saladin commanded a large army, and the letter to Archumbald credits Taqi al-Din with the decisive attack.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The army marched in divisions, with Raymond of Tripoli in the vanguard and the Templars in the rearguard. The relic of the True Cross was carried with it by the Bishop of Acre.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On Friday 3 July the army left Saffuriya and its supplies and marched under constant harassment. Short of the lake it halted and camped on dry ground, where the Muslims set fire to the brush around it. At dawn on Saturday 4 July Saladin attacked. The infantry fled to a hilltop, the knights were broken up around the True Cross, and the king was captured.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: De Expugnatione says Raymond advised against the march because of heat and lack of water, but Guy followed other counsel. The Lyon Eracles says the Templar master and Reynald of Châtillon urged battle. On 3 July Guy ordered the army to camp rather than push on to the lake.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The halt without water left a thirsty army surrounded overnight, and it could not fight effectively the next morning.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Guy, the Templar master and many knights were captured, and the True Cross was lost. Reynald of Châtillon was killed; the Lyon Eracles says Saladin killed him himself. De Expugnatione reports that captured Templars and Hospitallers were killed. Raymond, Balian of Ibelin and Reynald of Sidon escaped.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Within two months Saladin recovered most of the kingdom's inland cities and ports. Ashkelon fell in September, and Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Relieving a besieged town can draw a field army onto ground of the enemy's choosing. In summer campaigning, water decided the battle before the fighting began.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Latin accounts disagree on whose advice led the army astray: one Eracles version blames Raymond's proposed turn toward Hattin, another the Templar master and Reynald. De Expugnatione frames the defeat as divine punishment and favours Raymond, and some Latins suspected Raymond and Reynald of Sidon of collusion with Saladin.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: De Expugnatione is a partisan contemporary Latin chronicle. Edbury translates two versions of the Old French continuation of William of Tyre and a letter written less than two months after the battle. Dajani-Shakeel sets Hattin in the context of Saladin's recovery of Jerusalem, drawing on medieval Arabic accounts.

phases.title: Muster at Saffuriya
phases.description: The Frankish army gathers at the springs; Saladin besieges Tiberias.

phases.title: March without water
phases.description: The army marches east under harassment and halts on dry ground short of the lake.

phases.title: Night of fire
phases.description: Surrounded and thirsty, the camp is harassed by arrows and brush fires.

phases.title: Horns of Hattin
phases.description: Saladin attacks at dawn; the infantry breaks, Raymond escapes and the king is captured.

perspectives.name: Guy of Lusignan
perspectives.objective: Relieve Tiberias and defeat Saladin's invasion.
perspectives.known: Saladin was besieging Tiberias, and the countess in the citadel was appealing for help.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the army could cross the dry country to the lake under attack.
perspectives.constraints: A kingdom divided by noble rivalries, with conflicting advice from his council.
perspectives.forces: The royal host, Templars, Hospitallers, barons and mercenaries hired with Henry II's money.
perspectives.terrain: Dry uplands between the springs of Saffuriya and the lake in high summer.
perspectives.logistics: The army left its supplies at Saffuriya and carried little water.
perspectives.decision: He marched to relieve Tiberias, then ordered a halt on 3 July before reaching water.
perspectives.outcome: His army was destroyed, the True Cross was lost and he was taken prisoner.

perspectives.name: Saladin
perspectives.objective: Defeat the Frankish field army and recover the kingdom, including Jerusalem.
perspectives.known: The Frankish army had gathered at Saffuriya, beside reliable water.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the Franks would leave the springs to fight.
perspectives.constraints: The sources read describe his actions rather than his constraints, so this study does not reconstruct them.
perspectives.forces: A large army; the letter to Archumbald names his nephew Taqi al-Din as leading the decisive attack.
perspectives.terrain: Control of the ground and water between Saffuriya and the lake.
perspectives.logistics: The Lyon Eracles says water was poured out in sight of the thirsty Franks.
perspectives.decision: He besieged Tiberias, harassed the march, fired the brush around the camp and attacked at dawn.
perspectives.outcome: A decisive victory, followed within three months by the surrender of Jerusalem.

sources.title: Rashid al-Din, Jamiʿ al-Tawarikh: the battle of ʿAyn Jalut, trans. W. M. Thackston
sources.publisher: De Re Militari (Society for Medieval Military History)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Mongol forces under Hülegü took Baghdad in 1258 and put the last ʿAbbasid caliph to death. They then took Aleppo and Damascus, ending Ayyubid rule in Syria, and by 1260 had reached Gaza.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Mongols demanded the submission of the Mamluk sultan Qutuz; Britannica says he executed their envoy. In Rashid al-Din's Persian history of the Mongols, Qutuz consulted his amirs, one of whom, Bunduqdar, advised killing the envoys, and they were put to death that night. News of the Great Khan Möngke's death led Hülegü to withdraw with much of his army, leaving his general Kitbuqa in Syria with a smaller force.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Qutuz aimed to defeat the Mongol force in Syria before it could be reinforced. Kitbuqa had to hold the newly conquered lands with reduced strength.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Ain Jalut (Goliath's Spring) lay in the Jezreel Valley, beneath wooded hills where troops could be concealed. Beisan lay about 13 km away.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Kitbuqa's army included Syrian, Georgian and Armenian troops. Qutuz led the Mamluk army; Baybars, whom Qutuz had welcomed back from exile in Syria that year, led its vanguard, according to Rabie. Britannica's battle article describes the armies as roughly matched; EBSCO calls the Mamluk army vastly superior.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Mamluks positioned themselves so that the Mongols faced the rising sun and concealed much of their army in the hills. Kitbuqa kept his Syrian troops in reserve, fearing they might defect.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Mamluk army left Egypt in late July 1260, defeated a small Mongol force at Gaza and passed through Frankish territory near Acre. Rashid al-Din has Kitbuqa order his advance guard under Baidar to wait for him, and Qutuz drive it back before Kitbuqa arrived. On 3 September a Mamluk advance force provoked the Mongols and drew them into an ambush. The Mongols broke the Mamluk left wing, but the Mamluks rallied, Kitbuqa fell and the Mongols retreated to Beisan, where they were defeated again. Rashid al-Din has the fighting last from dawn until midday.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Franks of Acre declared neutrality and let the Mamluks pass and resupply, after a clash at Sidon had turned them against the Mongols. Kitbuqa chose to pursue the Mamluk advance force into the valley; in Rashid al-Din's account Qutuz feigned a withdrawal and sprang the ambush from three sides. Contemporary accounts say Qutuz threw down his helmet and rallied his men when the left wing gave way.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The ambush brought the concealed Mamluk army into action, and the rally after the left wing broke prevented a Mongol breakthrough. The defection of the Syrian auxiliaries then tipped the balance.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Kitbuqa was killed in battle or, by another account, captured and beheaded. Rashid al-Din has him refuse to flee when his men gave way, fall into Mamluk hands when his horse faltered, and be beheaded after defying Qutuz; Mongols hiding in a reed bed were burned. The Mamluks occupied Damascus and Aleppo and drove the Mongols out of Syria.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Mamluk rule extended from Egypt to the Euphrates. Qutuz was murdered on the way back to Cairo by a conspiracy formed by Baybars, who seized power; Rabie writes that Baybars had expected Aleppo as his reward and struck when Qutuz refused it. Mongol campaigns into Syria continued in later decades, and Mamluk offensives later took the remaining Frankish strongholds, ending with Acre in 1291.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Events far from the battlefield, such as a succession crisis, can change the balance of forces in a theatre. Knowledge of the ground can turn a familiar tactic against its masters.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources disagree on who directed the battle, Qutuz or Baybars, and on whether the Mamluk retreat was feigned or a regrouping; Rashid al-Din describes a feigned withdrawal, and Rabie credits Baybars with the vanguard. They also give different balances of strength and different accounts of Kitbuqa's death. Rashid al-Din, writing a history of the Mongols, gives Kitbuqa a hero's end and speeches that honour his loyalty, which should be read as the chronicler's portrait. Even the date varies: De Re Militari heads the excerpt 8 September but its introduction says 3 September, and Rabie places the battle loosely near Nablus. Britannica's claim that the battle saved Islam is a strong retrospective judgement.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives a narrative of the battle based on contemporary accounts. The EBSCO research starter gives political context, including the Frankish position, but contains some evident date errors, so it is used here only where it is consistent with Britannica. Rashid al-Din's Persian history, in Thackston's translation, gives the Mongol side. Rabie's Britannica biography of Baybars adds his part in the battle and the murder of Qutuz.

phases.title: Mongol advance
phases.description: Hülegü's forces take Baghdad, Aleppo and Damascus and reach Gaza.

phases.title: March north
phases.description: The Mamluk army leaves Egypt, defeats a Mongol force at Gaza and passes near Acre.

phases.title: Ambush at Ain Jalut
phases.description: An advance force draws the Mongols into the valley, where the concealed Mamluk army attacks.

phases.title: Rally and pursuit
phases.description: The Mamluks recover from a broken wing; Kitbuqa falls and the Mongols are beaten again at Beisan.

perspectives.name: Qutuz
perspectives.objective: Defend Mamluk Egypt against the Mongol advance.
perspectives.known: The Mongols had taken Baghdad, Aleppo and Damascus, but Hülegü had withdrawn with much of his army.
perspectives.uncertainty: How the Frankish states would respond to a Mamluk army crossing their territory.
perspectives.constraints: The need to move a large army north through Frankish lands before the Mongols could be reinforced.
perspectives.forces: The Mamluk army, with Baybars, who knew the terrain, among its generals.
perspectives.terrain: A valley overlooked by wooded hills in which much of the army could hide.
perspectives.logistics: The Franks of Acre allowed the army to resupply near the city.
perspectives.decision: He rejected Mongol demands and put the envoys to death, marched north and fought at Ain Jalut, rallying his men when the left wing broke.
perspectives.outcome: A decisive victory; he was murdered on the way back to Cairo.

perspectives.name: Kitbuqa
perspectives.objective: Hold Syria for the Mongols after Hülegü's departure.
perspectives.known: A Mamluk army was advancing north from Egypt.
perspectives.uncertainty: The loyalty of his Syrian troops, whom he kept in reserve for fear of defection.
perspectives.constraints: A reduced force, an uprising in Damascus that delayed him, and hostile Franks after his sack of Sidon.
perspectives.forces: Mongols with Syrian, Georgian and Armenian troops.
perspectives.terrain: He advanced into a valley facing the rising sun, with hills on which the enemy waited.
perspectives.logistics: The sources read do not describe his supply, so it is not reconstructed here.
perspectives.decision: He ordered an advance in pursuit of the Mamluk force; in Rashid al-Din's account he fought on after his army broke rather than flee.
perspectives.outcome: His army was defeated and he was killed or executed.

sources.title: The Siege of Constantinople in 1453, according to Kritovoulos (trans. Charles T. Riggs, 1954)
The Siege of Constantinople in 1453, according to Nicolo Barbaro (trans. John Melville-Jones, 1969)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the mid-15th century the Byzantine Empire held little more than Constantinople and the land just west of it, and the city's population had fallen to perhaps 40,000–50,000. The Ottomans controlled almost all of the Balkans and most of Anatolia, and Murad II had already besieged the city in 1422 before turning to a rebellion elsewhere.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Mehmed II, sultan again from 1451, made peace with Hungary and Venice in 1452 and built a fortress at the narrowest point of the Bosporus. Constantine XI appealed to the West. Hungary refused, and the pope pressed for church union, which the city's people resisted. Venice and Genoa sent help; 700 Genoese under Giovanni Giustiniani Longo arrived in January 1453, and Constantine gave him command of the land defences.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Mehmed meant to blockade the city by land and sea and batter its walls with cannon until he could break in or force a surrender before help came from Christian Europe. Constantine meant to hold the walls until that relief arrived.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The land walls ran about 6.5 km as a double line of ramparts behind a moat and had never been breached. Sea walls lined the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara, and a chain closed the mouth of the Horn. Kritovoulos says a long stretch of wall along the Horn, inside the chain, was left unguarded.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Estimates differ widely. Britannica cites the eyewitness Jacopo Tedaldi for 6,000–7,000 trained soldiers and 30,000–35,000 armed civilians in the city, against 60,000–80,000 Ottoman troops with 69 cannon and a fleet under Baltaoğlu Süleyman Bey. Barbaro puts the sultan's army at about 160,000. Mehmed commanded in person; Giustiniani led the land defence under Constantine.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Kritovoulos says Mehmed divided the walls among his commanders: Zaganos at Galata and the Horn, Karaja, Ishak and Mahmud on sections of the land wall, the sultan with his guard in the centre and Baltaoğlu with the fleet. Giustiniani concentrated most defenders on the land walls, and Barbaro records nine large ships placed along the boom on 9 April.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The bombardment began on 6 April, and an assault the next day was repelled. About 20 April a small relief convoy fought its way through the Ottoman fleet into the harbour. By 22 April Ottoman vessels had been hauled overland into the Golden Horn. Through May the besiegers mined under the walls while the defenders countermined. The general assault began before dawn on 29 May.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: After his fleet failed to force the chain, Mehmed had his smaller ships dragged on greased slipways over the hill behind Galata and into the Horn, stretching the defenders along yet more wall. For the final attack he combined artillery, infantry and ships, and sent in his Janissaries after two waves had been thrown back.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The defence broke when Giustiniani was wounded and carried from the walls, and his men left their posts. The sources disagree about how. Britannica says he was hit by gunfire and Kritovoulos says by a crossbow bolt, while Barbaro, a Venetian hostile to the Genoese, presents him as deserting and spreading a false alarm that the Turks were in.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Ottoman troops took the inner wall at the Gate of St Romanus and the city fell on 29 May 1453. A sack followed, which Kritovoulos describes in detail. Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia and made it a mosque. Accounts of Constantine XI's death differ: Kritovoulos has him fall fighting at the gate, while Barbaro reports only rumours.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Mehmed moved his capital from Edirne to Constantinople, resettled it with people of many faiths and styled himself Caesar of Rome, then campaigned through the Balkans and Greece. Christian Europe lost its eastern buffer and access to the Black Sea.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Walls that had held for a thousand years fell to a combination of sustained bombardment and complete blockade. Once the chain was bypassed, a small garrison was spread too thin, and its cohesion depended on a few leaders.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Each eyewitness writes from a side. Barbaro dwells on the Venetians and blames the Genoese, and Kritovoulos, who served Mehmed, is the Greek account most favourable to the Ottomans. Numbers vary several-fold between sources. Britannica reports that many scholars see the flight of Greek scholars to Italy as marking the end of the Middle Ages; that is a periodisation, not an event.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: This study uses translated extracts from Kritovoulos's History of Mehmed the Conqueror and Nicolo Barbaro's diary, with Britannica for the overall narrative. Other Greek historians of the fall, such as Sphrantzes, Doukas and Chalkokondyles, were not read here.

phases.title: Preparations
phases.description: Mehmed fortifies the Bosporus and has great cannon built; Giustiniani arrives with Genoese troops.

phases.title: Bombardment and blockade

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Babur, a descendant of Timur and of Genghis Khan, lost his father's principality of Fergana and failed to hold Samarkand against the Uzbeks. He seized Kabul in 1504 and between 1519 and 1524 raided the Punjab four times without gaining a firm hold; Lehmann writes that these raids showed him the dissension and mismanagement in the Lodi sultanate.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Ibrahim Lodi, sultan of Delhi from 1517, sought a centralised rule that alienated powerful nobles; the Lodi state had been built as a loose confederacy of Afghan and Turkish chiefs. Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of the Punjab, and Ibrahim's uncle Alam Khan urged Babur to invade a fifth time.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Babur set out in November 1525 to move against Ibrahim, who held Delhi and the dominions of Hindustan. Reports reached Babur that Ibrahim was advancing slowly to meet him, halting for days at each camp.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Panipat lies about 80 km north of Delhi. Babur rested his right on the town and its suburbs, put carts and mantelets across his front and protected his left with a ditch and felled branches. Gaps an arrow's flight apart let out 100 to 200 horsemen at a time.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Babur reports that Ibrahim's army was estimated at 100,000 men with about 1,000 elephants; Britannica's Babur article gives 100 elephants. Beveridge notes that Babur's army was 12,000 when it crossed the Indus, with later additions in the Punjab, and Babur says a count before the battle fell short of expectations.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Seven hundred carts were joined in the Ottoman fashion with rawhide ropes, with mantelets between them for matchlockmen. Humayun led the right and Muhammad Sultan Mirza the left, with a centre, an advance guard and a reserve. Turning parties (tulughma) stood at the tips of both wings to ride round the enemy's rear.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Humayun defeated Hamid Khan in February 1526, and on 2 April a detachment under Daud Khan Lodi was routed. Babur reached Panipat on 12 April and for a week harassed Ibrahim's camp; a night attack failed. On 20 April Ibrahim advanced at first light and by noon his army was broken. Babur reached Delhi on 24 April and Agra on 4 May.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: A council chose to fight from a fortified position anchored on the town. Babur then tried to provoke Ibrahim with raids and a night attack. When the enemy came on, he reinforced his right and ordered the turning parties to wheel round both flanks while the wings closed in.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: In Babur's account, Ibrahim's army halted on seeing the prepared line, unable either to stand or to keep advancing. The turning parties reached its rear, and its wings were crowded into the centre so tightly that they could neither attack nor escape. Lehmann describes an army that fought as an inflexible, undisciplined mass and quickly fell apart.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Ibrahim was killed and his body was found among the dead that afternoon; Babur later ordered a tomb built for him. Babur sent columns at once to secure the treasuries of Delhi and Agra, and the Friday sermon was read in his name in Delhi on 27 April. With Ibrahim dead, the Lodi confederacy dissolved.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle ended the Lodi dynasty and the Delhi sultanate and set the base for Mughal rule. Unlike Timur, Babur stayed; his men had expected another raid for booty, and he had to persuade them to remain. He faced Rana Sanga at Khanua in March 1527 with, Lehmann writes, virtually the same tactics in a far more closely contested battle.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A smaller army chose its ground, fortified it and let a larger one attack. Field defences, mobile flanking forces and missile fire worked together against an army whose commander could not rely on his nobles. Lehmann credits the discipline and mobility of Babur's troops, not superior weapons.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Babur dates the battle to 20 April, as does Lehmann; Britannica notes that some scholars prefer 21 April, the date its article on the Lodi dynasty gives. The role of guns is disputed. Britannica's battle article stresses artillery, but Beveridge argues that Babur had few guns, perhaps only two, and that he presents the victory as an archers' success; Lehmann also says his Ottoman experts had only two cannons at Panipat and that Babur did not introduce artillery to India. Babur's portrait of Ibrahim as miserly and untried is the victor's.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The main source is Babur's own memoir, written in Turki, in Beveridge's annotated translation, which compares manuscripts and earlier translations. Her notes also report an Afghan tradition that the fighting was unusually desperate. Britannica supplies the wider context, and Lehmann's Encyclopaedia Iranica article reads the campaign through the memoir.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi completed the unification of Japan in 1590. Before his death in 1598 he appointed five regents to rule for his young son Hideyori: Uesugi Kagekatsu, Mōri Terumoto, Maeda Toshiie, Ukita Hideie and Tokugawa Ieyasu.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Ieyasu's political marriages and his move to Ōsaka Castle led others to fear that he meant to supplant the heir. Ishida Mitsunari formed a coalition and on 22 August 1600 denounced him; Ieyasu answered with war. Alliances fell largely along east–west lines, but Uesugi in the east had plotted with Mitsunari: when Ieyasu marched against Uesugi in July, the National Park Service writes, Mitsunari hoped to lure him east, but Ieyasu left generals to hold Uesugi and moved on toward Edo at a slower pace.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Mitsunari aimed to preserve the Toyotomi legacy and stop Ieyasu. His plan was to hold the eastern army in the valley and then signal forces on the surrounding heights to descend and trap it. Ieyasu aimed to break the coalition and reunite his three columns in Mino province.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Sekigahara was a village in a mountain valley where several major roads met, among them the Nakasendō. Kobayakawa Hideaki's troops held Mount Matsuo to the south, and Mōri and Chōsokabe forces held Mount Nangū behind the eastern army. A thick fog covered the valley until about 8 a.m.; the National Park Service has visibility of about 100 feet when fighting began.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Britannica gives Ieyasu nearly 89,000 men against just under 82,000 for the western coalition, including 15,000 under Kobayakawa; the National Park Service treats the two armies as roughly equal. Both armies were coalitions of daimyō under their own lords. Turnbull warns that the standard troop layouts derive from an 1893 General Staff reconstruction based on cruder old maps.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The western army arrived first after a night withdrawal from Ōgaki Castle. Ukita held the centre, Shimazu Yoshihiro the north and Ōtani Yoshitsugu the south, with Mitsunari behind field fortifications on Sasaoyama. Ieyasu entered from the Nakasendō road and set his headquarters on Momokubari hill, with Fukushima Masanori in the vanguard and Ii Naomasa's shock troops.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Ieyasu's columns converged on Mino; the defenders of Fushimi Castle held the western army from 27 August to 6 September, Gifu fell, and Ieyasu's son Hidetada was delayed besieging Ueda Castle. On 21 October fighting began in the fog, about 7:30 a.m. by the National Park Service's account, when Ii Naomasa charged ahead of Fukushima. At 11 a.m. Mitsunari signalled Kobayakawa, who stayed still until shortly after noon and then attacked Ōtani. Other units defected, the western centre broke, Shimazu withdrew, and by 2 p.m. Ieyasu declared victory.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: At Ōgaki on the eve of battle, the National Park Service writes, Shimazu proposed a night attack, which Shima Sakon called dishonourable; Mitsunari agreed with Shima and withdrew to Sekigahara instead. Ieyasu attacked into a valley overlooked by enemy forces because he had secret assurances from Kobayakawa and Kikkawa Hiroie. Ōtani turned half his men to face Kobayakawa in expectation of betrayal. Kikkawa's refusal to move held back the Mōri and Chōsokabe troops behind him.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Kobayakawa's attack on Ōtani and the defections that followed broke the western line, and Kikkawa's inaction held back some 20,000 Mōri and Chōsokabe troops. Shimazu, too, refused to join the fight when Mitsunari rode to him. Shiramine Jun, as reported by Turnbull, argues that the defection came at the start of the battle rather than at midday.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The western coalition was shattered. Shimazu's men cut their way out through the eastern army. Mitsunari fled into the mountains and was beheaded in Kyōto within a month, and Ieyasu took Sawayama and Ōsaka castles within days.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Ieyasu confiscated lands from opponents and rewarded allies, including Kobayakawa and Kikkawa. In 1603 the emperor appointed him shōgun, founding a shogunate that lasted until 1868, and in 1615 the siege of Ōsaka destroyed the remaining Toyotomi, including Hideyori.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: The battle was largely decided by negotiation before it began; a plan that depended on allies obeying a signal was only as strong as their loyalty. Turnbull also stresses that it was one battle in a wider war, in which events at Fushimi, Gifu and in the north could have changed the result.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Turnbull reports Shiramine Jun's 2014 revision: early reports called the battle Yamanaka, the labels Eastern and Western army appear only in 1698, the story of Ieyasu firing on Kobayakawa is a myth, the hill units were waiting on events, and the battle was shorter. Turnbull finds the defection timing persuasive. Britannica and the National Park Service follow the conventional account; the Park Service presents the volley at Kobayakawa's troops, Ii Naomasa's ruse and Kikkawa's idleness as plain narrative.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the conventional narrative and Turnbull summarises recent Japanese research. The National Park Service's chapters on the campaign and the battle give a fuller conventional account, timed through the day. Shiramine's book and the Japanese primary sources were not read directly.
